While you do that, here are the defaults I plan to use. Tell me if any are wrong.

**Size:** `e2-small` (2 shared vCPU, 2 GB RAM) in `us-central1-a`, 20 GB disk, Debian 12, with a reserved static IP.
- This is the smallest size I'd trust. Synapse, Postgres, LiveKit and the TLS proxy together will run out of memory on the 1 GB `e2-micro` as soon as you join a large room.
- It should cost roughly $15–20/month including the IP. I'll confirm the exact price before creating anything.

**Calls:** The Fold's group calls will use MatrixRTC with a LiveKit media server, using Element Call's end-to-end encryption. The encryption keys travel over Matrix, so the media server only forwards encrypted media and can't read it. One-to-one calls will go through the same server.

**Stack in Docker Compose:** Synapse, Postgres, LiveKit, `lk-jwt-service`, and Caddy for automatic HTTPS.

**Firewall:** TCP 80 and 443, TCP 7881 and UDP 7882 for LiveKit, and SSH only from your IP. Federation port 8448 stays closed.

**Privacy:** Federation off and registration closed, which suits a law firm. Accounts would be created by an admin, or by The Fold through the admin API.

**I need two things from you:**
1. **The hostname for the homeserver**, for example `matrix.rklacylaw.com` or a Fold domain. It becomes the server name in every Matrix user ID, such as `@alice:yourdomain`, and can't be changed later.
2. **Where that domain's DNS is managed** (Cloud DNS in this project, Squarespace or Google Domains, Cloudflare, etc.). I need to add A records, or have you add them, before Caddy can get certificates.

A browser chat surface for The Fold. It runs like the fold does — a static
page, no build step, deployable to GitHub Pages — and it is the chat the
Fold has always implied: **models are organs behind Heimdall, the chat is the
mouth, and nothing raw leaves the trust domain.**

## What this is

LibreChat-style chat (artifacts, memory, search, agents) is the long game. But
LibreChat itself is a Next.js server that needs MongoDB + Redis — it cannot run
as a static GitHub Pages site. So this repo is the Fold-native chat surface
that speaks the **same OpenAI-compatible wire LibreChat speaks**, pointed
straight at the one process that already routes the whole Fold's models:

```
  fold-chat (browser, static)
        │  GET /api/tags            → every model heimdall can serve
        │  POST /v1/chat/completions (SSE, heimdall_privacy:"sealed-external")
        │  POST /api/code             (the code lane — same bridge, same project)
        ▼
  heimdall bridge  (localhost:8790)
        │  fleet · linked native hosts · remote providers
        │  sealed-external gate + dispatch ledger + savings meter
        │  the machine door: khora read → janus derive → execute → penelope retain
        ▼
  local organs (WebLLM, Ollama, phones)  ·  outside models (sealed projection only)
```

## One thread, one project, two engagements

Chat and Agent are **sibling engagements over a shared session**, not one app
embedded inside another (the Claude / Claude-Code shape). The **mode** row of the composer's
"this turn" chip switches what a turn *does*; it never changes the thread, the store, or the
project:

- **Chat** answers from the routed models (`/v1/chat/completions`).
- **Agent** dispatches the same turn through the same bridge to the **machine
  door** (`/api/code`) — the khora conductor, which reads the project, derives
  over it with janus, executes for real, and retains the trace with penelope.
  Its tool activity and answer render inline in the one conversation, in the
  agent's own register: a teal rail, a mode tag, a terminal composer, and a
  labelled seam where the thread hands off between the two engagements.

The two engagements convert freely: any chat answer can be **built** (the same
ask re-run through the machine door) and any agent artifact can be **explained**
(the same ask re-run through the grounded chat lane), and every message carries
a per-message **run as** affordance. A conversion only adds a lane to the same
thread — the original turn and its record are never overwritten.

A **project** is the shared container: a name, an optional **folder** (the
working directory an agent turn is bound to), and a preset its sessions inherit.
A chat turn and an agent turn hang off the same project, so both start from the
same place. Projects support create / settings / delete.

Every agent turn carries an **agent record** (the same collapsed disclosure a
chat turn carries): the folder, the lane, the tool steps, the time — so the
agent is as inspectable as chat, and always says it ran through the bridge.

Serve `index.html` from localhost (`python3 -m http.server 8814`) and run
`heimdall up` — the page finds the bridge on `localhost:8790` and lists every
model heimdall can serve. For code, run the conductor door
(`khora/native/conductor/server.mjs`) and start heimdall with
`HEIMDALL_OPENCODE=http://127.0.0.1:4098`. The GitHub Pages deployment is the
same page; full model access needs the local bridge, exactly like the fold's own
local serving.

text:
There are two things to separate here. Which option is best depends on whether you want a server in the path at all.

**Why the Synapse relay is the wrong shape.** Any server that fetches a URL on a user's behalf sees the URL, the query and the page, and its IP is the one in the destination's logs. Matrix encryption can't change that, because the relay has to decrypt the request to make it. Your current Worker is already that kind of exit point. [fold-chat-web.js:31](fold-chat-web.js:31) points at `holodeck-proxy…workers.dev`, and my probe shows `/raw?url=` answers with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. So anyone's site can route arbitrary fetches through that account. That open proxy is your real liability exposure today, not the VM I was about to build.

**Ways around CORS, from least to most operator involvement:**

1. **Fetch through the local bridge (my pick).** The page already requires the heimdall bridge on `localhost:8790` for models. Add a fetch/search endpoint there. Node has no CORS, requests leave from the user's own IP, and you're nowhere in the path. Watch for Chrome's local-network permission prompt, and Safari may block an https page calling `http://localhost`.
2. **Browser extension.** An extension with host permissions can fetch any site with no CORS. The page talks to it by message, and no server is involved. The cost is install friction and store review for broad permissions.
3. **Bring-your-own Worker.** Each user deploys a 40-line stateless Cloudflare Worker and pastes its URL into settings. The relay and the liability sit with the person using it.
4. **Direct calls to sources that already send CORS headers.** I confirmed these send them: Wikidata, PubMed, Europe PMC, Stack Exchange, Open Library, DuckDuckGo Instant Answer, and CourtListener (useful for a law context). These do not: arXiv, DuckDuckGo HTML search, SearXNG, and Federal Register. Open-web search and arbitrary page reads are exactly what a browser page can't do alone, so 1–3 cover that part.
5. **Matrix as a blind mailbox (the one case where the VM still fits).** The browser, say on a phone, sends encrypted requests to the user's own heimdall node. Synapse only carries ciphertext, and the fetch happens on their machine. This is the only setup where "we store nothing about requests" is actually achievable. Synapse would still see sender, room and timestamps, which retention limits and log suppression can shrink but not remove.

Things that don't work: `fetch` with `mode: "no-cors"` (the response is opaque), iframes, and service workers.

I'd also stop shipping the public CORS proxies (allorigins, corsproxy.io, codetabs and others in [fold-chat-web.js:39](fold-chat-web.js:39)) as defaults. Make them opt-in, so no outside party sees every page a user reads without their say-so.

**Status:** I created nothing in GCP. The only change is that `admin@rklacylaw.com` is signed in again.

**Decision for you:** should I drop the VM and implement option 1 in the bridge, then the extension? Or do you want option 5 for remote and phone use, in which case I'd build `the-fold` as an ephemeral, log-free Synapse?

text:
Yes, you can run a server-like thing in the browser, but it can't fix CORS.

**What you can run in a tab:**
- **Service Worker:** it answers requests to your own origin, which is useful for offline or PWA behavior.
- **WebContainers (StackBlitz):** a full Node.js runtime in WASM.
- **v86 or CheerpX:** a whole Linux VM in WASM.
- **Dendrite compiled to WASM:** a Matrix homeserver in the browser. It was a P2P Matrix demo, and I haven't checked whether it's maintained.

**Why it doesn't help:**
- **The sandbox still applies.** Everything in the tab, including a Linux VM, sends its network traffic through the browser's own `fetch`. A Node server inside the page is blocked by CORS exactly as the page is today.
- **No listening, no raw sockets.** The page can't accept inbound connections or open arbitrary TCP/UDP. These VMs only reach the internet through a relay server, which puts you back at hosting one.
- **WebSockets and WebRTC don't help.** A WebSocket isn't subject to CORS, but the target site has to speak it, and ordinary sites don't. WebRTC only connects to other peers, which is useful for linking a phone to the user's own machine but not for fetching web pages.
- **The one browser-side exception is Direct Sockets.** It's a Chrome API for installed Isolated Web Apps, which is a heavy requirement for something users just open.

To call sites that don't allow it, something has to run outside the browser sandbox. That is the local bridge, an extension, or a desktop wrapper, which are options 1 and 2 from my last message. If you want zero hosting and zero liability, those two are the answer, not a virtual server.

Want me to start on the bridge endpoint (option 1)? The heimdall bridge isn't in this repo, so I'd need its folder, and I haven't found it yet. Or I can sketch the extension, which would live in this repo. Either way I'd leave the GCP VM alone.

text:
This fits The Fold well, and it removes the need for the VM.

**Why it fits**
- **The page is already extension-shaped.** There's no build step, no `eval`, no remote imports, and the icons are vendored. Models sit behind heimdall, so no WebLLM is bundled. The only MV3 blockers are the two inline `<script>` blocks, at [index.html:8](index.html:8) and [index.html:789](index.html:789). Both move into small files.
- **CORS stops applying.** An extension page with `host_permissions` can fetch cross-origin directly. The fetch is already injectable, as `outbound.auditedFetch` at [fold-chat.js:1677](fold-chat.js:1677), so almost nothing changes. The outbound audit ledger keeps working and now truthfully records that calls go from the user's machine.
- **The bridge gets easier.** A host permission for `127.0.0.1:8790` removes the CORS, mixed-content and Chrome local-network-prompt problems. That makes Safari's `localhost` blocking moot.
- **The relay chain goes away.** `FOLD_RELAY` and the public proxies in [fold-chat-web.js](fold-chat-web.js) aren't needed. No server and no third party sees a read, so you hold nothing about users' requests.
- **New capability.** A side panel beside any page can read the user's open page or selection directly, with no fetch at all.

**Decisions and risks**
1. **Permissions.** `<all_urls>` triggers the "read all your data on all websites" install warning and slow review. Better is a fixed host list for the direct sources and search providers. Arbitrary page reads would use per-site `optional_host_permissions`, requested on a user click.
2. **The fetcher becomes a privileged tool driven by a model reading hostile pages.**
   - Always use `credentials: "omit"`, so it never rides the user's logged-in sessions (client portals, email).
   - Allow https only, and refuse loopback and private addresses except the bridge.
   - Re-check after redirects, and cap size and time.
   - Never expose it to web pages, so no site can use the extension to reach someone's LAN.
   - Chrome can't see DNS answers, so the private-address check is best-effort.
3. **Distribution.** MV3 forbids remotely hosted code, so each change goes through a store (an unlisted listing is fine) instead of an instant Pages deploy. The firm's own machines can force-install by policy. Keep the static site as a demo, with a platform check choosing plain fetch in the extension and the current path on Pages.
4. **Reach.** Desktop Chrome, Edge, Brave and Firefox work. Safari needs an Xcode wrapper. Phones mostly can't use extensions (Firefox for Android can). Reaching your home machine from a phone is the only case that still justifies a Matrix mailbox, and I'd defer it.
5. **State.** The extension's `localStorage` and IndexedDB are separate from the Pages origin, so existing chats won't carry over. It needs a one-time export/import.

I haven't created anything in GCP, so the VM question is moot.

I can build a spike here: an MV3 `manifest.json` with side panel and full-tab entry, the two inline scripts moved out, and the host permissions. It would also add a small `fold-chat-exit.js` for the fetch rules above, with `node --test` coverage. Then you load it unpacked and I check DuckDuckGo search end to end. Want me to start?

  extension page's CSP refuses (inline script, `on*=` handlers, remote scripts, unresolved imports). The two inline

The Fold now builds as a Chrome extension that fetches from the user's own machine, with no relay and no VM. I loaded the built extension into a real Chromium and tested it there. The full unit suite passes (620 tests, 0 failing), and the browser run held except for the points below.

```bash
node scripts/build-extension.mjs   # then chrome://extensions → Developer mode → Load unpacked → dist/extension
```

**What the browser test showed**
- **Boot and gate:** the page boots with no CSP violations. The exit gate sits on the page's `fetch`, and it refused `http`, IP addresses, `localhost`, `*.local` and POST.
- **Search and relay:** Brave answered 12 of 12 searches, with a median of about 620–650 ms in two runs. No request went through the relay or a public proxy.
- **Artifact isolation:** artifact code runs in a sandbox page with no extension API and no access to chat storage.
- **Permissions:** reading arbitrary websites is off by default, and the person turns it on from the options page.

**Things you should know**
- **A file I overwrote:** I overwrote `fold-chat-engines.js`, which another session was creating at the same moment. I recovered it exactly from that session's transcript, and its tests pass. Sessions that touch this repo have also been told.
- **Brave rate limit:** my test runs (about 45 searches from your IP in under an hour) got Brave answering 429 with a captcha. I stopped sending it traffic, so the second pre-registered check is incomplete: 17 of 18 pages read, out of the 36 planned.
- **Misleading error:** the engines module reports that 429 as "markup may have changed". I wrote this up in `experiments/source-routing/RESULTS.md` and told its owner.
- **Search engines:** DuckDuckGo challenges every query, so Brave is the only working engine. Both engines still receive every query.
- **Artifact previews:** they won't run in the extension until three `srcdoc` lines in files owned by another session are swapped for `sandboxDoc()`. I sent the exact patch.
- **Provider keys:** calling model providers directly with user-supplied API keys would be blocked by the gate. It would need an explicit allowlist.
- **Not done:** icons, a store listing, and Firefox or Safari support.
- **Commits:** I didn't commit anything. Another session already committed my first files.

**GCP:** nothing was created, and the Synapse idea is dropped. Separately, the `default` network leaves SSH, RDP, VNC and ports 3000 and 4000 open to the internet on every VM, including the running n8n and hyphae machines. That's worth fixing. The details are in the new files [the-fold-extension-and-shared-tree.md](/Users/mlacy/.claude/projects/-Users-mlacy-Library-Application-Support-Claude-scratch-workspaces-4bf59fed-b26b-4f7d-a90f-11d28a16ba25-1a7b49f0-7962-48a4-8bfc-8a3bc2e27d2d-scratch-2026-10-05-a25b81/memory/the-fold-extension-and-shared-tree.md) and [gcp-utility-emitter-project.md](/Users/mlacy/.claude/projects/-Users-mlacy-Library-Application-Support-Claude-scratch-workspaces-4bf59fed-b26b-4f7d-a90f-11d28a16ba25-1a7b49f0-7962-48a4-8bfc-8a3bc2e27d2d-scratch-2026-10-05-a25b81/memory/gcp-utility-emitter-project.md) in my memory notes.
